en: The Hymn to Avalokiteśvara composed by Carapati.
Om. Homage to Avalokiteśvara.

O Lord of the World, whose feet are honored by gods, humans, and asuras, who has overcome birth, old age, sickness, and death—protect me, who am without refuge; O Compassionate One, exercise your mercy! (1)
Perceive me, submerged in the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra and shattered by the great waves of the afflictions;
do not disregard me as I cry out—save me, O Great Compassionate One! I bow to you. (2)

O Blessed One, protect me; look upon me while I have not yet fallen into the treacherous Avīci hell—my eyes afflicted by the cataracts of craving, my body overwhelmed by the great terror of death. (3)
I have repeatedly taken other women’s wives and killed thousands of creatures unknowingly. O Lord, now destroy all that physical evil, the sin committed by me.
O Lord of the World, pacify all that verbal hell, long practiced by me, which consists of the untruths I have constantly spoken to people for the sake of livelihood and honor. (5)
O Lord, now shatter this mental sin of mine—the evil thought of sentient beings here, which I myself approved and even committed as a human being—as I utter this lamentation. (6)

"Among the classes of gods, humans, and asuras, and those in the realms of animals, hell-beings, and pretas—whatever beings dwell there, always afflicted, you protect them; such is the report concerning you that has reached me. (7)
"Therefore, show compassion toward me, seeing the youth residing in my body.
Listen to this, O Blessed One, as I speak it while I have not yet entered hell. (8)
Moreover, O Blessed One, having approached, why do you abandon me while my purpose remains unfulfilled?
Or rather, having observed my merit, you generate compassion; how could that which has been seen not result in success?
You are fully satisfied even by mere remembrance, and you cast away impurity; why then have you not been seen?
Therefore, O Blessed One, expert in the welfare of others, do not delay; protect me here! 10.
A kingdom consisting of elephants, horses, sons, and wives—a palace of manifold splendor free from thorns;
even unto its very bones, heads, blood, and flesh, you have given it to supplicants in infinite measure. (11)

The accomplishment of collyrium, pills, and magical sandals; the purification of perfected medicines, jewels, and mantras; and the entry into the city of Yakṣa women—all these are achieved for one whom you, O Lord of the World, find pleasing. 12.

Those who are deprived of hands, feet, and eyes, and who are wretched from the great fear of various diseases—when you are pleased, they sport about with healthy bodies, free from illness, and profound in virtue. (13)
Poison, disease, planetary spirits, and dākinīs are always pacified by the yoginīs;
the messenger of Yama does not pass before him for whom you, O Jina, are pleased. (14)

Thus, O Lord of the World, why do you abandon me, the protectorless, while I am being attacked? Day after day I cry out with uplifted hands, my voice agitated by terror; destroy [my fear], O Blessed One! (15)
With a mind agitated by the senses and their objects, and having committed many sins with a distracted heart, I have spent this entire life in vain, wandering for the sake of the belly alone. (16)

Therefore, O Lord of the World, act now for me; here I am, bowing with my hands joined in various salutations, so that without experiencing the faults of the miserable states, I may attain a good rebirth from you, yet not [yet] final liberation. (17)
You are the cause for the destruction of delusion and hatred, the bridge across the great ocean of saṃsāra;
you are the one who raises his arm to lift up those fallen in fear, and you are the Rāhu that swallows the moon of heavy sins. 18.
You have taught the unsurpassed reality of the Sugata; you have protected many suffering beings;
you have conquered the invincible Māra of passion; you have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of existence. (19)
You are the one whose body severs all worldly speech; you possess a sublime body that has contemplated the entire universe.
O Blessed One, you are an incomparable ocean of compassion, known by people as a friend without cause.
You have effortlessly shattered the fragmentation of karma; you are devoted to the welfare of others;
with your mind absorbed in divine meditation, you regard supplicants with an impartial heart. (21)
Even while performing the greatest service for me, you, though compassionate, find no satisfaction in me;
how can this unwholesome and fallen body, bitten by the great serpent of delusion and ensnared by the objects of the senses, be acceptable? (22)
Is that compassion which you have toward the welfare of all beings not extended to you with certainty? For why do you not protect me, a sinner, as I cry out before you? (23)

O Lord, your compassion is as vast as space; for toward sentient beings it flows like a stream from a cloud, moving incessantly and without interruption across all lands—whether dry or watery, low or high—in every region.
By whatever merit I have gained from this recollection of the Blessed One, may this entire world obtain residence on the mountain of Śrī Potalaka and produce beautiful and manifold delights. 25.
The hymn to the venerable lord Śrīmad-Āryāvalokiteśvara, composed by Carapati-pāda.
